motion: Does divine hiddenness count against a perfectly loving God?

bridges.description: Show why nonresistant unbelief counts against a perfectly loving God that seeks relationship.
Show why even one genuine nonresistant nonbeliever contacts the universal loving-God claim.
Ask why a loving God leaves intellectual belief as a barrier to relationship or salvation.
Show how hiddenness remains compatible with a perfectly loving God's purposes and justice.
Challenge public confidence that nonresistance can be identified despite desire-laden belief formation.
Separate present propositional belief from relationship and ultimate salvation, including possible postmortem reconciliation.

sections.title: Scope of the hiddenness challenge
sections.rationale: Both sides delimit the motion to a perfectly loving God rather than generic theism.

sections.title: The one-exception claim and its probability
sections.rationale: This section tests whether one nonresistant case is enough and whether such a case has adequate support.

sections.title: Postmortem reconciliation
sections.rationale: Jones offers eventual reconciliation as a compatibility response and Paulogia tests its theological basis.

sections.title: Private experience and public evidence
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute whether hiddenness is independent public evidence or a personal conclusion.

sections.title: Introspection and personal force
sections.rationale: Paulogia's stated openness and Jones's conclusion-versus-argument reply bear directly on personal rational force.

sections.title: Loving disclosure and unequal evidence
sections.rationale: Paulogia argues that a loving God should bridge an open person's gap; Jones limits the public reach of that report.

sections.title: Belief, relationship, and salvation
sections.rationale: The final burden concerns whether present belief is a necessary gateway and whether eventual justice answers hiddenness.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: The argument need only conclude that no perfectly loving God exists, rather than that no God exists.
moves.warrant: Gods without loving attributes are conceivable, so the unrestricted opening and conclusion are unnecessary.
moves.inference: Hiddenness can count against the loving-God claim without purporting to refute generic theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Paulogia's proposed simplification and ends after his explicit narrowed conclusion, preserving the complete reason for removing both outer premises.

moves.importanceRationale: This fixes the exact proposition Paulogia undertakes to support.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly defines the pro side's motion-level claim.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: Divine hiddenness challenges Christian theism but does not refute basic deism or generic theism.
moves.warrant: Jones identifies his earlier response as Christian in scope and expressly agrees that the argument does not debunk God's existence in general.
moves.inference: The dispute should assess compatibility with the loving Christian God rather than treat hiddenness as universal disproof.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Jones's complete scope agreement and ends before Paulogia changes to the terminology question.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it doesn't debunk a general existence of God
moves.attributionRationale: Turn ownership is clear from the named handoff, first-person continuity, and the surrounding guest exchange.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Even one capable person who is nonresistantly in unbelief gives divine hiddenness evidential force.
moves.warrant: The formulation requires at least one such person; studies about a vast majority being influenced do not establish that everyone is resistant.
moves.inference: A population tendency cannot answer a universal one-exception challenge.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span preserves Paulogia's quoted formulation, one-person inference, and contrast between a vast majority and everyone through his direct question.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: even if there is only one person that falls in this category
moves.attributionRationale: Turn ownership is clear from the named handoff, first-person continuity, and the surrounding guest exchange.

moves.importanceRationale: The one-exception logic is central to the pro burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It states why a single genuine case contacts the loving-God claim.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: The relevant question is whether a genuinely nonresistant person is probable, not merely conceivable.
moves.warrant: Failure to show bias on one tested belief does not show freedom from desire in other beliefs; Jones nevertheless allows the hypothetical possibility.
moves.inference: Without evidence moving possibility toward probability, the one-person premise lacks sufficient public support.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage includes Jones's reading of the studies, his conditional allowance, and his explicit possibility-versus-probability distinction.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: The claim that an honest nonbeliever may receive another opportunity after death needs a theological basis.
moves.warrant: The Christian traditions familiar to Paulogia admired C. S. Lewis but did not hold that an honest nonbeliever receives another chance.
moves.inference: The compatibility response depends on support beyond merely asserting postmortem reconciliation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage identifies the C. S. Lewis issue and ends with Paulogia's focused request for scriptural or theological derivation.
moves.attributionRationale: Turn ownership is clear from the named handoff, first-person continuity, and the surrounding guest exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks whether later reconciliation can remove the present belief barrier.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: Postmortem salvation is a scripturally and philosophically possible answer, though its mechanics remain speculative.
moves.warrant: Jones cites passages he interprets as limiting guilt where law or knowledge is absent and as allowing preaching to the dead, while admitting that claims beyond death are speculative.
moves.inference: If eventual informed reconciliation remains possible, present hiddenness need not conflict with perfect love.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Jones's complete initial answer, including the cited interpretive basis and his explicit speculation qualification, before Paulogia raises Romans 1.
moves.attributionRationale: Jones's ownership is clear, but automatic captions materially corrupt names and several biblical references.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the cited names and biblical references if their exact wording becomes material; no quotation is selected from corrupted terms.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies a major compatibility model with an explicit uncertainty limit.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers eventual reconciliation as a route by which hiddenness and love coexist.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: Divine hiddenness is either a personal experiential report or a conclusion derived from other evidence, rather than an independent public argument.
moves.warrant: A believer's report of experiencing Jesus and an atheist's report of not experiencing Jesus are both subjective; alternatively, perceived insufficiency of other evidence leads to the hiddenness conclusion.
moves.inference: Neither form independently establishes that a perfectly loving God does not exist.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins when Jones returns to hiddenness, preserves both branches of his distinction, and ends with his concise summary of the objection.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's more of a conclusion not the arguments itself

moves.importanceRationale: This is Jones's main account of why hiddenness lacks independent public force.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the con side's motion-level public-evidence objection.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: The cited psychology supports a tendency, not a universal rule, and leaves room for the single exception the argument needs.
moves.warrant: Some participants shifted counter to desire; a ten-to-two pattern and a small minority are not zero.
moves.inference: Majority bias does not defeat an argument requiring only one genuine nonresistant case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Paulogia's numerical and subgroup response and ends with his explicit point that the study does not cover every decision by every person.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: small doesn't mean 0 and 10 to 2 doesn't mean everyone

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: After honest introspection, Paulogia sees no attachment he would refuse to surrender and says he would return to Christianity if the intellectual problem were resolved.
moves.warrant: He reports having lived well as a Christian and leaving because of an intellectual problem rather than a desired lifestyle change.
moves.inference: His apparent openness supplies a concrete candidate case for personally rational nonresistant unbelief.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span resumes after the excluded joke at Paulogia's guest-only clarification and preserves his complete introspective deconversion and conditional-return example.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: if I became convinced of it I'd become a Christian again

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: Paulogia's account is a conclusion reached from other intellectual considerations, not an independent hiddenness argument.
moves.warrant: The intellectual problem did the argumentative work; describing God as hidden follows from that prior assessment.
moves.inference: Personal rational force does not automatically become public evidence against theism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Jones's direct characterization of Paulogia's account and his complete conclusion-versus-argument distinction.
moves.attributionRationale: Turn ownership is clear from the named handoff, first-person continuity, and the surrounding guest exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It denies that the personal account independently proves the motion.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: A loving God has provided much stronger evidence to some people, so failing to bridge an open nonbeliever's gap counts against perfect love.
moves.warrant: Biblical figures received direct visions or encounters, and such disclosure need not destroy freedom because even fully informed beings can reject God.
moves.inference: Unequal evidence makes the continued personal gap evidentially relevant when the person remains willing to relate.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes Paulogia's unequal-evidence examples, his free-will answer, and his present conclusion while retaining his qualification that a future plan remains possible.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the only conclusion I can draw is that there is no loving

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: A report that God has not bridged one person's gap remains private evidence others cannot independently assess.
moves.warrant: Just as another person's religious experience cannot compel an outsider, Jones cannot inspect Paulogia's feelings or cognitive state.
moves.inference: Public conclusions must be argued from evidence accessible in other ways.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage includes Jones's full analogy to religious-experience debates and his conclusion that neither side's private report becomes objective public evidence.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones
moves.claim: Even if honest rejection exists, a perfectly loving and just God can eventually forgive, heal, and provide missing information.
moves.warrant: Jones says postmortem salvation is possible, perfect love and omniscience imply perfect justice, and an honest nonbeliever would ultimately be made right.
moves.inference: A present nonresistant case does not entail permanent relational loss or contradiction with love.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts with Jones's answer to the possibility question and preserves his justice inference, eventual-information claim, and return to the public/private limitation.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: If belief is a prerequisite to salvation or relationship, a loving God should provide enough disclosure that no willing person remains blocked at that stage.
moves.warrant: Making God known differs from compelling the person's later relational or moral choice.
moves.inference: Removing the intellectual barrier would enable rather than determine a person's response.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Paulogia's obligation question and ends after he clarifies that disclosure should prevent unbelief, before the mixed-turn repair of his wording.
